actions.text: Hello everyone, and welcome to our class! Today we're starting something really interesting. Picture this: you're at a playground, and two groups of kids both rush toward the same ball at the exact same moment. What happens next? Let's find out together.

actions.content: The playground scene: two groups, one ball, same moment.

actions.text: Look at the scene here. Group A and Group B both want that one ball. Before we decide who's right, let's just watch the moment happen. Who do you think should get the ball?

actions.content: This slider is where you decide how Group A responds.
Group A chooses to acknowledge the other group instead of ignoring them.

actions.text: You're in charge of this slider. Group A can ignore the others, listen to them, or try to solve it together. Let's start by having Group A truly listen. Watch the children's faces and feelings change — and predict first: will both groups feel better, or only one?

actions.content: This box shows what the children say and how they feel after your choice.

actions.text: Notice something important here. Disagreeing about a ball doesn't mean one group is the problem. Both groups just want to be heard. Keep asking yourself: what if both sides could feel listened to? That question is exactly where we're heading next.

That question from our last page — what if both sides could feel heard? — is exactly what we'll test now. Here is the same playground moment, with the same two kids. Only the mindset changes. Let's look at the controls first.

actions.content: Choose which mindset the two kids bring to this moment.

actions.text: Watch the sliders underneath. They show two important things: how much I stand up for what matters to me, and how much I consider what matters to my friend. Keep your eyes on both as we change the mindset.

actions.content: First mindset: I give up what matters to me so my friend is happy.

actions.text: Here is Lose-Win. I drop what matters to me so my friend gets what they want. My friend looks happy — but look at my side of the seesaw. Is that really a win for both of us? Press play and see how it feels.

actions.content: Second mindset: I get my way, and my friend loses out.

actions.text: Now Win-Lose. I get my way, but it comes at my friend's expense. Noticing the pattern? In both of these, someone gets ignored. So what would it look like if we cared about both?

actions.content: Third mindset: we both hold on to what matters.

actions.text: That is Win-Win. We consider what matters to both of us, so both sliders stay high. One thing to remember: these are response patterns we choose, not labels for people. Try Lose-Lose too and see what happens when nobody cares about anybody — then bring your favorite pattern to our next page, where we find the two skills that make Win-Win possible.
We just saw three mindsets — and you figured out that Win-Win is the one where both people matter. Now let's find the two skills that make it possible. Watch the diagram build itself.

actions.content: Courage steps in first — I say what matters to me.
Consideration joins it — I listen to what matters to you.

actions.text: Here is the tricky part. Courage on its own can sound pushy. Consideration on its own can turn into giving in and feeling grumpy. So what happens when the two work together? Let's look at each side of the circle.

actions.content: My side: what do I really want?
Your side: what do you really want?
Where the two circles overlap, something brand-new can grow.

actions.text: See that glow in the middle? That is the Shared Solution — an idea neither of us had on our own. Tap the Fair Agreement node and you will meet Ava and Ben, who both want the tablet after dinner. Ava does not get the whole evening, and Ben does not either. They get something better: twenty minutes each, and an agreement they can both say yes to. That is the secret — courage plus consideration. On our next page, you will try it yourself on a real choice.

We just said the secret is courage plus consideration. Now let's use it for real. Maya wants to watch a movie, and Arjun wants to go to the park. They are both your friends, and today you get to help them talk it out.

Notice the middle space between them. That is where both friends sit together. Watch it closely, because a Win-Win idea has to land right there — a choice that is fair, possible, and agreed by both of them.

actions.content: The shared middle: where agreement grows.
Patience drains while the game runs — don't waste it.

actions.text: Here is your challenge. Drag the move cards onto your friends. Try listening first, then sharing how they feel, then brainstorming something new. If you push one friend into agreeing, or you give in for them, is that really Win-Win? Watch the happy meters and the agreement bar to find out.

actions.content: Start when you are ready — listen before you decide.

elements.content:
• Express what you want

• Respect family limits

• Divide the tasks

• Use each strength
Reflect: What could you say so both feel heard?

actions.text: You did a great job on the movie-or-park challenge. Now we bring Win-Win out of the game and into real life. This is our last stop today: Think Win-Win Everywhere. Let's look at two everyday situations.

Situation one: clothing and the family budget. Maybe you really want that new jacket, or those shoes everyone is wearing. Win-Win here means two things. You express what you want — you say it clearly and politely. And you respect the family's limits. That is courage and consideration working together: speak up, and listen too.

Situation two: the poster contest. Here is the good news — nobody has to lose. Divide the tasks, and use each strength. The classmate who loves drawing designs the poster. The one who writes well does the words. The one who is good at speaking presents it. When everyone uses their strength, the whole team wins.

And here is our key takeaway. Think Win-Win. Five small steps: Listen. Express. Consider. Explore. Agree. Listen to the other person first. Express what you need. Consider how they feel. Explore some ideas together. Then agree on something that works for both of you. Remember these five words and you can use Win-Win anywhere.

Take a quiet moment with this last question. Think of a time when you and someone wanted different things. What could you say or do so both of you feel heard? Hold on to that question. You have all done wonderful work today — you learned the three mindsets, courage plus consideration, and now how to think Win-Win with your friends and your family. Try it once this week, and watch what happens.

actions.topic: What could you say or do so both people feel heard?
actions.prompt: Think of a time you and someone wanted different things. Share one sentence you could say that shows both courage and consideration.
